items.syllabus_item: 1.1 Various types of drawings with their importance and uses

body.en:
Drawing is the language of the engineer. A building cannot be described fully in words: sizes, shapes, positions and relations of hundreds of parts are communicated by drawings — scaled, conventional pictures read the same way by the architect, engineer, contractor, mason and the approving authority. IS 962 is the Indian code of practice for architectural and building drawings. One building job passes through a family of drawings, each made for a different reader and purpose.

1) Preliminary / sketch drawings. Freehand or rough scaled sketches made while the idea is forming: room arrangement (the line plan), rough sizes, alternatives compared. Importance: cheapest stage to change anything; errors corrected here cost nothing, the same change after construction costs a demolition.

2) Presentation drawings. Neat, attractive drawings — coloured plans, elevations, 3-D and perspective views — made so the client (who may not read working drawings) can understand and approve the proposal. Use: approval of concept, loans, brochures.

3) Submission (approval) drawings. Drawings submitted to the sanctioning authority (municipal corporation, urban development authority) in the prescribed format and colour code: site plan, floor plans, elevation, sections, area statement and FSI calculations. Use: legal permission to build — Unit 2 covers their bye-laws.

4) Working (construction / execution) drawings. The most important set for the diploma engineer: fully dimensioned plans, elevations, sections, foundation plan, structural (RCC) details, schedules of openings, services layouts — everything the site needs to build without asking questions. Use: setting out, quantity estimation, construction and checking. Unit 3 is devoted to preparing these.

5) Detail / shop drawings. Large-scale drawings (1:20 to 1:1) of one component — staircase, door, window, footing, reinforcement — prepared by the contractor or fabricator from the working drawing. Use: fabrication and exact execution of that part.

6) Record (as-built) drawings. Working drawings corrected after construction to show what was actually built (shifted walls, buried pipelines, cable routes). Use: maintenance, repair, extension and legal record for decades.

7) Other working companions. Location/site plans fix the building on its plot with roads and boundaries; tender/contract drawings form the legal basis of the contractor's rates; structural drawings (prepared by the structural engineer) and services drawings (water supply, drainage, electrical) complete the set a building is actually built from.

The reading rule. No single drawing is complete alone: the plan gives lengths and widths, the elevation gives heights as seen, the section gives heights and construction as cut, the schedules and notes give what geometry cannot. A good reader keeps cross-checking views against each other — the habit Unit 3 trains.

items.syllabus_item: 1.2 Types of projections adopted: 1.2.1 First angle, 1.2.2 Third angle, 1.2.3 Combination of first and third, 1.2.4 Advantages and disadvantages of each, 1.2.5 Situations where each is used

body.en:
Why projection is needed. A drawing sheet is flat (2-D); a building is solid (3-D). Orthographic projection shows the solid as separate true-shape views — what we call plan (top view), elevation (front view) and side elevation — obtained by looking squarely at each face and projecting it onto a plane. The two standard arrangements of these views are first-angle and third-angle projection; they differ only in where each view is placed on the sheet.

First-angle projection (1.2.1). The object is placed between the observer and the plane. The view is projected through the object and drawn on the opposite side: the top view (plan) is placed below the front view, the view from the left is placed on the right. Think of the object rolled away from you: what you saw from above lands underneath.

Third-angle projection (1.2.2). The plane is between the observer and the object (like looking through glass). Each view is drawn on the same side from which it is seen: plan above the front view, left-side view on the left. The arrangement therefore looks 'natural' — each view sits next to the face it shows.

Combination of first and third (1.2.3). In building drawing practice the strict placement rules are relaxed into a practical combination: the plan is drawn below the elevation (first-angle habit) but sections and side elevations are placed wherever the sheet layout is clearest, each labelled (Section AA, Side Elevation) so no confusion arises. Building views are large and few, and every view is titled — the drawing stays unambiguous even when view placement follows sheet convenience.

Advantages and disadvantages (1.2.4). First angle: standard in India and Europe (IS 962 / BIS practice), matches the building-trade habit of plan-below-elevation; disadvantage — beginners find opposite-side placement confusing for small machine parts. Third angle: views adjacent to the face seen, easier for a beginner to visualise, standard in the USA; disadvantage — not the Indian building convention, and mixing it unknowingly into an Indian submission set creates misreading. The real danger is never the system itself — it is a drawing with no projection symbol and unlabelled views.

Situations where each is used (1.2.5). First angle: all Indian civil/architectural drawings (this subject), structural drawings, GTU examinations. Third angle: American drawings and much machine-drawing/CAD work originating in the USA. The projection symbol (two circles beside a frustum/trapezoid — see the diagram) printed near the title block declares which system the sheet uses; check it before reading any imported drawing.

Reading rule for buildings. In this subject: plan below, elevation above, section beside, every view titled and dimensioned. If a view could be mistaken, it gets a label — the combination method of 1.2.3 with discipline.

items.syllabus_item: 1.3 Symbols, Conventions and Abbreviations: 1.3.1 materials of construction, electric fittings, water supply and sanitary, furniture, graphical symbols for doors and windows; 1.3.2 abbreviations used for the above

body.en:
Why symbols exist. A plan at 1:50 cannot draw a real brick course, a real WC or the swing of a real door at true detail — and need not. Standard symbols and conventions (IS 962) replace repeated detail with agreed signs, so every reader decodes the same meaning. Four families appear in the syllabus.

1) Materials of construction (in section). Where a section cuts material, the cut face is hatched or shaded by convention: brickwork — horizontal course lines (often shown red in submission drawings); cement concrete — scattered dots and small triangles; earth/soil — 45° diagonal hatching; stone/rubble — irregular wavy closed outlines; timber — wavy grain lines; glass — two/three thin parallel diagonal lines; steel — solid black or double lines. The hatch instantly tells the reader what the cut part is made of without a written label on every wall.

2) Doors and windows (graphical symbols). In plan, a door is drawn as a gap in the wall + a leaf line + a quarter-circle swing arc: the arc shows the opening direction and the clear space the door sweeps (1.5 will schedule D1, W1…). A double door has two leaves and two arcs; a sliding door is a leaf drawn inside the wall thickness with an arrow. A window is drawn as three parallel lines within the wall thickness (outer frame lines + glass line); ventilators similar, smaller and placed high. These symbols decide furniture placement — a door swing must never be drawn through a bed or basin position.

3) Water-supply and sanitary fittings. Plan symbols: WC (Indian/European pan outline with cistern rectangle), wash basin (oval/D-shape with tap dot), sink (rectangle with inner rectangle and drainer lines), bath tub, shower (square with diagonal spray lines), floor trap/nahani trap (small square/circle with cross), taps and valves (small bow-tie/circle signs on pipe lines), underground pipe lines shown dashed with W/S labels. Bath-WC layout in Units 2–3 is read entirely in these symbols.

4) Electrical fittings and furniture. Electrical: switch (dot with inclined tick), socket outlet, ceiling light point (circle with cross), fan (circle with blade marks/F), distribution board (labelled rectangle DB), one-way runs as thin lines to the switch. Furniture conventions (bed, table, sofa, wardrobe, kitchen platform) are drawn as thin outline rectangles in presentation/line plans to check clearances — not in working plans, where they would clutter dimensions.

Abbreviations (1.3.2) — the working set. A drawing cannot repeat long words in every note, so standard abbreviations are used (capital letters, no full stops): PL plinth level, GL ground level, FFL finished floor level, CL centre line, RCC reinforced cement concrete, PCC plain cement concrete, DPC damp-proof course, WC water closet, WB wash basin, GS kitchen sink, NH nahani (floor) trap, CI cast iron, GI galvanised iron, PVC/uPVC plastic pipes, SW stoneware (drainage), DP down pipe (rain water), MH manhole, IC inspection chamber, FSI floor space index, D/W/V door/window/ventilator in schedules. Notes combine them: '75 mm SW DP at corner, to IC then MH' is one complete instruction to the plumber.

Exam habit. Symbol questions ask you to draw the symbol and name it — practise the actual sketch (hatch, swing arc, WC outline), not only the description. Keep the swing arc dotted/thin and the leaf as a clear line; keep hatching inside the cut face only.

items.syllabus_item: 1.4 Types of lines: visible lines, centre line, hidden line, section line, dimension line, extension line, pointers, arrow head or dots

body.en:
Lines are the words of the drawing. Every line type has a fixed thickness and dash pattern (IS 962 / SP 46 practice) so that the kind of line itself carries meaning before a single word is read. Using the wrong line is a spelling mistake that changes the sentence.

Visible (object) line. Thick continuous line. Every edge and outline that can be seen in that view: wall faces in plan, building outline in elevation. This is the strongest line on the sheet — the hierarchy starts here.

Hidden line. Medium line of uniform short dashes. Edges that exist but are hidden behind something in this view: foundation edges under a floor plan, the far side of a window opening, concealed beams. Dashes must start and end with a dash at the feature, with small gaps at corners.

Centre line. Thin chain line — long dash, short dash, alternating. Marks axes and centres: column/wall centre lines, centre of circles and symmetric parts. It extends a little beyond the feature on both sides and is the first line drawn when laying out a plan (the grid).

Section (cutting-plane) line. Chain line made thick at the ends (and at direction changes), with arrows showing the direction of viewing and letters (A–A, B–B) naming the section. In the section view itself, the cut faces are bounded by thick lines and hatched (Card 1.3); parts beyond the cut are drawn as ordinary visible lines, thinner in feel.

Dimension line. Thin continuous line carrying one size: placed outside the outline wherever possible, with arrowheads (small filled triangles, about 3 mm long) touching the extension lines — or dots/oblique ticks where space is tight (architecture often uses 45° ticks). The figure is written above the line, upright, in mm, and never struck through by the line.

Extension (projection) line. Thin continuous line drawn from the feature (with a small gap from the outline) out to the dimension line. It projects the exact points between which the size is measured.

Pointer / leader line. Thin line from a note to the exact part it describes, ending in an arrowhead on an edge (or a dot inside a surface). The note end carries a short horizontal shoulder. Leaders prevent long notes being written across the drawing.

Companion lines of the set. Break line (thin freehand or zig-zag) — a long part is 'broken' to fit the sheet; phantom line (long dash + two short dashes) — alternate position of a moving part (door swing path is a civil example) or adjacent parts; property/boundary lines in site plans shown chain-thick; hatching lines thin at 45° inside cut faces only.

Thickness discipline. A drawing uses roughly three weights: thick (≈0.5 mm) for visible cut outlines, medium (≈0.3 mm) for visible uncut outlines and hidden lines, thin (≈0.18 mm) for dimension, extension, centre, leader and hatch lines. Printed boldness must follow importance — if dimensions shout louder than walls, the sheet is wrongly 'spelled'.

items.syllabus_item: 1.5 Scale: 1.5.1 Definition, 1.5.2 Scales used for various types of drawings, 1.5.3 Sizes of various standard papers

body.en:
Definition (1.5.1). A building cannot be drawn full size, so it is drawn in fixed proportion: the scale is the ratio between a size on the drawing and the same size on the actual object. It is stated as a Representative Fraction (RF) — the same ratio as a pure number:

RF = (size on drawing) / (same size on object) — both in the same unit

Scale 1:50 (RF = 1/50) means 1 mm on paper represents 50 mm on site; a 6000 mm wall is drawn 6000/50 = 120 mm long. Three families: full scale 1:1 (small components), reducing scales (RF < 1 — all building drawings), enlarging scales 2:1, 5:1, 10:1 (tiny details such as joinery sections). On a printed/photocopied set the written scale fails if the sheet is resized — which is why every drawing also carries written dimensions: 'do not scale the drawing, follow figured dimensions' is a standard note.

Scales used for various drawings (1.5.2) — the working table. Site/location plans: 1:1000, 1:500 (sometimes 1:2000 for layouts). Submission and working floor plans, elevations, sections: 1:100 for large buildings, 1:50 the usual residential choice (this subject's sheets). Foundation and structural layouts: 1:50. Staircase, toilet and kitchen details: 1:20. Joinery, footing and RCC component details: 1:20, 1:10, 1:5. Full-size moulding profiles: 1:1. Choose the largest scale that fits the sheet with room for dimensions and notes — readability decides, habit second.

Sizes of standard papers (1.5.3). Drawing sheets follow the ISO A-series, each size exactly half the previous (folded along the long side): A0 841 × 1189 mm, A1 594 × 841 mm, A2 420 × 594 mm, A3 297 × 420 mm, A4 210 × 297 mm. GTU drawing examinations and this subject's practicals use A2/A1 sheets for buildings and A3 sketchbooks for symbols and components. Every sheet carries a border, and a title block (bottom-right, typically 185 × 65 mm region) recording project, drawing title, scale, date, drawn/checked names and sheet number — the sheet's identity card.

Sheet layout discipline. Plan, elevation and section of one job are arranged so views align (plan below elevation sharing the same vertical projectors where possible); margins keep drawings off the border; north point and scale are stated on site/floor plans; revision clouds and a revision table record changes. A neat sheet is not decoration — it is error control.

title.en: Numerical 1.1 — From scale to site size, and from sheet size to plot size
title.gu: Numerical 1.1 — From scale to site size, and from sheet size to plot size

body.en:
Given. A floor plan is drawn to scale 1:50. On the sheet, a room measures 96 mm × 78 mm. The plot on a 1:500 site plan measures 24 mm × 40 mm.

Find. (a) The actual room size. (b) The actual plot size and plot area.

Step 1. Convert the room length using the scale ratio.

actual length = drawing length × scale denominator = 96 × 50 = 4800 mm = 4.80 m

Step 2. Convert the room width the same way.

actual width = 78 × 50 = 3900 mm = 3.90 m

Step 3. Convert the plot sides at 1:500.

plot side 1 = 24 × 500 = 12000 mm = 12.0 m ; plot side 2 = 40 × 500 = 20000 mm = 20.0 m

Step 4. Find the plot area from the actual sides (never multiply sheet area directly — convert lengths first, or use the area ratio RF²).

plot area = 12.0 × 20.0 = 240 m²

Final answer.

╔ Room = 4.80 m × 3.90 m ; Plot = 12.0 m × 20.0 m = 240 m² ╗

Validity check. Area check by RF²: sheet area = 24 × 40 = 960 mm²; 960 × 500² = 240,000,000 mm² = 240 m². Both routes agree. Remember: lengths scale by RF, areas by RF², volumes by RF³.

title.en: Numerical 1.2 — Choosing a scale that fits the sheet
title.gu: Numerical 1.2 — Choosing a scale that fits the sheet

body.en:
Given. A house is 11.4 m long × 8.6 m wide. It must be planned on an A3 sheet (420 mm × 297 mm) keeping about 40 mm total margin/border allowance in each direction, so the usable drawing area is about (420 − 40) × (297 − 40) = 380 mm × 257 mm. An elevation of height 3.6 m must also fit vertically if placed on the same sheet.

Find. The largest standard scale (1:20, 1:50 or 1:100) that fits.

Step 1. Find the RF demanded by the length (the controlling, longer side).

RF needed ≤ 380 / 11400 = 1 / 30 → denominator must be ≥ 30

Step 2. Test 1:20 — its denominator 20 is less than 30, so it is too large.

drawn length at 1:20 = 11400 / 20 = 570 mm > 380 mm ✗ does not fit

Step 3. Test the next standard scale, 1:50, for both directions.

length = 11400 / 50 = 228 mm ≤ 380 mm ✓ ; width = 8600 / 50 = 172 mm ; height = 3600 / 50 = 72 mm ≤ 257 mm ✓

Final answer.

╔ Use scale 1:50 (at 1:100 every size halves — it fits, but wastes the sheet and loses detail) ╗

Validity check. Rule of this subject: pick the largest standard scale that fits with margin. 1:50 keeps doors, windows and dimensions readable; 1:100 is reserved for larger buildings or smaller sheets.

q.en: What is a working drawing?
q.gu: What is a working drawing?

a.en: The fully dimensioned drawing set (plans, elevations, sections, details, schedules) from which the building is actually constructed on site.
a.gu: The fully dimensioned drawing set (plans, elevations, sections, details, schedules) from which the building is actually constructed on site.

q.en: Which projection is used for Indian building drawings, and where does the plan sit?
q.gu: Which projection is used for Indian building drawings, and where does the plan sit?

a.en: First-angle projection (IS 962); the top view (plan) is placed below the front view (elevation). In practice, building sheets use the labelled combination.
a.gu: First-angle projection (IS 962); the top view (plan) is placed below the front view (elevation). In practice, building sheets use the labelled combination.

q.en: What does the projection symbol on a sheet tell you?
q.gu: What does the projection symbol on a sheet tell you?

a.en: Whether the sheet uses first-angle or third-angle projection, so views are not misread. It is placed near the title block.
a.gu: Whether the sheet uses first-angle or third-angle projection, so views are not misread. It is placed near the title block.

q.en: Draw/describe the plan symbol of a single door.
q.gu: Draw/describe the plan symbol of a single door.

a.en: A gap in the wall, the door leaf as a line at one jamb, and a thin quarter-circle arc showing the swing/opening direction.
a.gu: A gap in the wall, the door leaf as a line at one jamb, and a thin quarter-circle arc showing the swing/opening direction.

q.en: How is a window shown in a plan?
q.gu: How is a window shown in a plan?

a.en: As three parallel lines within the wall thickness - frame lines and the glass line.
a.gu: As three parallel lines within the wall thickness - frame lines and the glass line.

q.en: What is a hidden line used for? Give one civil example.
q.gu: What is a hidden line used for? Give one civil example.

a.en: To show edges hidden in that view - e.g., foundation edges below a ground-floor plan, shown as medium short dashes.
a.gu: To show edges hidden in that view - e.g., foundation edges below a ground-floor plan, shown as medium short dashes.

q.en: What is the difference between a dimension line and an extension line?
q.gu: What is the difference between a dimension line and an extension line?

a.en: The dimension line carries the size figure between arrowheads; extension lines project the measured points from the feature out to the dimension line.
a.gu: The dimension line carries the size figure between arrowheads; extension lines project the measured points from the feature out to the dimension line.

q.en: Define RF and give the RF of scale 1:50.
q.gu: Define RF and give the RF of scale 1:50.

a.en: RF = drawing size / actual size in the same units. For 1:50, RF = 1/50 = 0.02; 1 mm on paper = 50 mm on site.
a.gu: RF = drawing size / actual size in the same units. For 1:50, RF = 1/50 = 0.02; 1 mm on paper = 50 mm on site.

q.en: What do the abbreviations FFL, DPC and SW pipe mean?
q.gu: What do the abbreviations FFL, DPC and SW pipe mean?

a.en: FFL - finished floor level; DPC - damp-proof course; SW - stoneware (pipe used for underground drainage).
a.gu: FFL - finished floor level; DPC - damp-proof course; SW - stoneware (pipe used for underground drainage).

q.en: Why is 'do not scale the drawing - follow figured dimensions' written on drawings?
q.gu: Why is 'do not scale the drawing - follow figured dimensions' written on drawings?

a.en: Prints and photocopies can shrink or stretch, so measured sizes become wrong; the written figures remain the legal sizes.
a.gu: Prints and photocopies can shrink or stretch, so measured sizes become wrong; the written figures remain the legal sizes.
